title: The choreography of teaching 30 children at the same time
author: Tom Sherrington
summary: Effective whole-class teaching requires deliberate choreography: intentional orchestration of student engagement so all learners remain active participants. The core challenge is ensuring every student—not just most—is thinking, making meaning, and practicing at all times. This demands four engagement modes: whole-class instruction, individual teacher-student engagement, peer engagement, and independent work. Success requires systematic attention to: engineering full attention through accountability and cold calling; addressing prior knowledge gaps through common experiences and scaffolding; using generative tasks (Think Pair Share, explain-the-answer routines) so students self-assess understanding; checking understanding across the whole class via sampling and circulation; establishing a culture of error where mistakes become learning opportunities; and responsive verification loops where reteaching confirms learning transfer. Guided and independent practice must maintain high success rates through scaffolding and flexible pathways.
points: Whole-class teaching requires intentional choreography across four engagement modes to ensure all students learn simultaneously
Engineering full attention demands cold calling, high accountability, and deliberate scanning rather than relying on volunteers or hand-raising
Generative tasks (Think Pair Share, explain-the-answer) are essential so students discover gaps in their own understanding before advancing
Checking understanding must be systematic and whole-class, not sampling a few students; Show-Me Boards and circulation are critical tools
Responsive verification loops ensure that when errors are identified, reteaching actually closes the gap for struggling learners
quotes: In my opinion the practicalities - the mechanics, the routines - of running a room so that every single individual in it is learning, are not sufficiently examined and spelt out in our training and professional discourse.
How will I make sure EVERYONE is learning? [The key question underlying all choreography decisions]

Students do not learn simply by being in a room where other people are learning. They each need to be active participants and, if we want to ensure learning is happening, we need to check that it is – for everyone.

The key is to engineer full attention intentionally, not assume it. It's natural and inevitable that students – with their pesky human brains – will mind-wander unless they have a strong pull to concentrate.

Instead of looking for some correct answers or fully correct/excellent responses the explicit goal is to find out who got things wrong and to explore what the underlying issues are.” Archived from Teacherhead on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
